 Hard-core Halloween celebrators will get an extra hour of partying — and early-birds will get an extra hour of sleep — this weekend when Daylight Saving Time ends .
 Clocks will be set back an hour early Sunday morning, from 2 a.m. to 1 a.m., which occurs every year on the first Sunday of November. But it is a rare occurrence that Halloween coincides with the time change.
 For the two events to take place in the same weekend, Oct. 31 must fall on a Saturday, which won't happen again until 2037 .
 For those who plan to party late into the night, that means an extra hour in costume, out on the town or celebrating with friends. For those with an earlier bedtime, DST grants you an extra hour of sleep as you recover from Halloween candy sugar crashes.

 History of Daylight Saving Time
 In observance of DST, clocks are turned forward one hour on the second Sunday in March. This causes there to be more light in the evening and less light in the morning during the spring, summer and part of fall.

 In November, clocks are turned back again to provide more light in the morning and less light in the evening. The winter months' earlier sunsets is a topic of debate for many, as less light during the time of year when much of the country is cold and snowy makes for a gloomy and bleak atmosphere.
 DST began as a way to make the most of available daylight, with the first implementations recorded in Europe during World War I. The U.S. also adopted DST during war times, but it wasn't until 1966 when it was standardized across the country in the Uniform Time Act. The act stated that DST would run from the last Sunday in April to the last Sunday in October.
 In 2007, DST was moved to its current schedule of March through November.
 Other countries have adopted DST year-round, or abolished it completely, and the pros and cons of these options have been a longstanding debate in the U.S. Each state is allowed to opt out of DST , as Hawaii and Arizona have, but they can't implement any alternatives.
 Legislation proposing permanent DST passed unanimously in the Senate in 2022, but the House never voted on it.
 As such, turning the clocks back an hour to end DST remains on the calendar for this weekend in West Virginia. However you feel about DST, I hope you find a way to enjoy its rare overlap with the spookiest night of the year.
